hints: Focus on the two comparisons given: right ventricle pressure is lower than the right atrium above it AND lower than the pulmonary artery ahead of it.
Remember the golden rule for valves: a valve opens when pressure behind it is higher and pushes it open, and it snaps shut when pressure ahead of it is higher to stop backflow.
walkthrough:
**Picture the right side of the heart**

Think of blood flow in one direction: right atrium -> right ventricle -> pulmonary artery. Valves sit between these chambers to keep flow one way.

The atrioventricular (tricuspid) valve is between atrium and ventricle. The semilunar (pulmonary) valve is between ventricle and artery.

**Check the atrioventricular valve**

We are told pressure in the right ventricle is lower than in the right atrium. That means higher pressure is pushing from behind, from atrium to ventricle.

Higher pressure behind pushes the valve open, so blood can fill the ventricle. So AV valve is open.

**Check the semilunar valve**

We are also told pressure in the right ventricle is lower than in the pulmonary artery. That means higher pressure is ahead, in the artery.

If the valve were open, blood would flow backwards. So the valve stays closed to prevent backflow. So semilunar valve is closed.

**Match to the table**

Open AV valve plus closed semilunar valve matches row C. This is ventricular filling (diastole), when the ventricle is relaxed and filling up.

options.A: Both closed would mean no filling and no ejection. But atrium pressure is higher than ventricle, so the AV valve must be open to allow filling.
options.B: This is backwards. Ventricle pressure is too low to push the semilunar valve open, and atrium pressure is high enough to push the AV valve open.
options.C: Correct. Higher atrium pressure opens the AV valve for filling, while higher artery pressure keeps the semilunar valve closed to prevent backflow.
options.D: Both open never happens. If the semilunar valve were open with artery pressure higher, blood would flow backwards into the ventricle.
